# Volume 2 — XIX Just a Happy Day

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“When it comes down to it,” Nell had formerly remarked to Thirza, “I feel that the most delightful and charming days are not the ones where something exceptionally grand, marvelous, or thrilling takes place, but simply those offering modest small delights, coming softly one after another, akin to pearls sliding from a thread.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0000 }

An existence at Grey Shutters consisted of precisely those kinds of days, because the adventures and misadventures of Nell, much like those of everybody else, failed to occur all at the same time, being instead scattered throughout the year with extensive periods of safe, joyful days in between, packed with labor, daydreams, merriment, and schooling. Towards the end of August, one of those days arrived. During the morning, Nell alongside Isolde used a rowboat to take the thrilled twins down the pond toward the sandshore so they could gather “sweet grass” and wade through the surf, above which a ancient song, mastered when the earth was new, was being played by the wind.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0001 }

During the afternoon, Nell made her way to the old Stanhope place so she could visit Cedric. Beside the dense fir grove offering protection to the north side of the house, she discovered him lying extended on the grassy bank, completely engrossed in a fairy-tale book. Upon catching sight of her, he leaped to his feet with radiant joy.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0002 }

“Oh, teacher, your arrival makes me so happy,” he said with enthusiasm, “since Grandma is not here. Won't you remain and share tea with me? Having tea completely alone feels so lonely. You understand, teacher. I truly considered requesting that Young Mary Joe join me at the table for her tea, although I anticipate Grandma would not like that. According to her, the French must be kept where they belong. Furthermore, conversing with Young Mary Joe is hard. She simply chuckles and remarks, ‘Well, yous do beat all de kids I ever knowed.’ My notion of conversation is not that.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0003 }

“Naturally I will remain for tea,” Nell stated cheerfully. “I was longing for an invitation. Ever since I previously had tea in this place, I have been craving another taste of the mouthwatering shortbread made by your grandma.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0004 }

Cedric appeared extremely grave.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0005 }

“Were it up to my own wishes, teacher,” he remarked, remaining in front of Nell while keeping his hands inside his pockets as an unexpected look of concern clouded his lovely small face, “I would gladly give you shortbread. However, Mary Joe is the one who decides. Before departing, Grandma was overheard by me instructing her that I was not to be allowed any shortcake since it was excessively rich for the stomachs of young boys. Even so, Mary Joe might perhaps slice a portion for you provided I give my word not to consume a bite. We should wish for a favorable outcome.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0006 }

“Yes, let us,” concurred Nell, who found this optimistic outlook entirely to her liking, “and if Mary Joe turns out to be ungenerous and refuses to hand over any shortbread it is of no consequence whatsoever, which means you must not feel anxious about it.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0007 }

“Are you certain it won’t bother you if she fails to do so?” Cedric asked in an anxious manner.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0008 }

“Absolutely certain, my love.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0009 }

“In that case, I will not be anxious,” Cedric remarked, exhaling deeply in relief, “particularly because I truly believe Mary Joe will hear reason. Naturally, she is not an unreasonable individual, yet experience has taught her that going against Grandma’s commands is a mistake. Grandma is a fine woman, but folks are required to obey her. She felt extremely delighted with me earlier today since I finally contrived to consume my entire plate of porridge. Succeeding required a major exertion. Grandma remarks that she believes she may still turn me into a man. However, teacher, I need to pose a most critical query to you. You are going to give me an honest reply, aren't you?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0010 }

“I’ll try,” Nell promised.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0011 }

“Am I out of my mind, do you believe?” inquired Cedric, as though her response held the weight of his entire life.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0012 }

“Goodness, no, Cedric,” Nell uttered with surprise. “You definitely are not. Whatever made you think that?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0013 }

“Mary Joe . . . however, she was unaware that I overheard her. The hired girl of Mrs. Peter Mott, Veronica, visited Mary Joe yesterday evening, and their conversation in the kitchen reached my ears while I traversed the hall. I overheard Mary Joe remark, ‘Dat Cedric, he is de queeres’ leetle boy. He talks dat queer. I tink dere’s someting wrong in his upper story.’ For a very long time last night, I was unable to sleep because I was pondering her words and questioning whether Mary Joe could be correct. Somehow, I was unable to bring myself to question Grandma regarding the matter, yet I resolved to query you instead. It brings me such joy that you believe the upper story of my mind is completely fine.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0014 }

“Naturally you are. Mary Joe is a foolish, uneducated girl, and you must not ever trouble yourself over whatever she tells you,” Nell declared with indignation, privately deciding to subtly suggest to Mrs. Stanhope that it would be wise to curb Mary Joe’s speech.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0015 }

“Well, that eases my worries,” Cedric remarked. “Thanks to you, teacher, I am completely contented at present. Having a flaw in your head wouldn't be pleasant, would it, teacher? Mary Joe probably thinks I do because I occasionally share my thoughts about things with her, I presume.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0016 }

“That is quite a perilous thing to do,” acknowledged Nell, drawing from her personal background.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0017 }

“Well, eventually I will share with you the ideas I expressed to Mary Joe, and you may judge on your own whether they contain anything strange,” Cedric said, “however, I am going to delay until dusk starts to fall. That happens to be the period when I long to disclose things to others, and whenever no one else is around, I simply must confide in Mary Joe. But following this, I will refrain from doing so if it causes her to think my mind is unbalanced. I will simply suffer the longing in silence.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0018 }

“And should the pain become overly severe, you may travel to Grey Shutters to share your ideas with me,” proposed Nell, employing the complete seriousness that made her beloved by youngsters, who truly adore being treated earnestly.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0019 }

“Yes, I will. However, my wish is that Robin is absent upon my arrival, as he pulls expressions at me. It does not bother me greatly since he is a mere child while I am rather grown-up, yet having expressions pulled at one remains disagreeable. Furthermore, Robin pulls exceptionally dreadful ones. At times, I fear his expression will remain permanently distorted. He pulls them toward me during service, precisely when sacred matters should occupy my thoughts. Lucy enjoys my company, nevertheless, and I enjoy hers, albeit less than prior to her revealing to Posy Fay Pembroke her intention of marrying me upon my reaching adulthood. Although I might wed someone once I am grown, I remain entirely too youthful to contemplate such things presently, wouldn't you agree, teacher?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0020 }

“Quite young,” concurred teacher.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0021 }

“Mentioning marriage brings to my mind a different matter that has been bothering me recently,” Cedric went on. “On a day last week, Mrs. Sowerby came over to have tea alongside Grandma, and Grandma forced me to display the portrait of my little mother to her . . . the picture sent by father as my birthday gift. Showing it to Mrs. Sowerby wasn't something I really wished to do. Mrs. Sowerby is a good, kind woman, yet she lacks the qualities of someone you would choose to see your mother's image. You understand, teacher. Naturally, however, I did as Grandma instructed. Mrs. Sowerby remarked that she was extremely pretty yet appeared rather actressy, and had to be a great deal younger than father. After that, she inquired, ‘Some of these days your pa will be marrying again likely. How will you like to have a new ma, Master Cedric?’ Truly, that thought left me nearly breathless, teacher, yet I refused to allow Mrs. Sowerby to notice it. I simply stared directly into her face . . . in this manner . . . and I replied, ‘Mrs. Sowerby, father made a pretty good job of picking out my first mother and I could trust him to pick out just as good a one the second time.’ And teacher, I truly can trust him. Even so, I desire that, should he ever provide me with a new mother, he will seek my thoughts regarding her prior to it being too late. Mary Joe is approaching to summon us for tea. I am going to talk over the shortbread with her.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0022 }

Because of the “consultation,” Mary Joe divided the shortbread and included a dish of preserves on the menu. Nell served the tea, and she and Cedric enjoyed an extremely cheerful meal inside the dark old sitting room with its windows unclosed to the winds from the gulf, and the pair conversed with so much “nonsense” that Mary Joe felt rather shocked and mentioned to Veronica the following night that “de school mees” matched Cedric in being strange. Following tea, Cedric brought Nell to his bedroom so he could display his mother’s portrait, which served as the secret birthday gift Mrs. Stanhope had stored inside the bookcase. Cedric’s small room with its low ceiling formed a gentle swirl of reddish illumination originating from the sun going down over the ocean and moving shadows produced by the fir trees growing near the square, deeply set window. Emerging from this soft radiance and enchantment was a lovely, youthful face possessing gentle mother eyes, which hung upon the wall located at the bed's foot.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0023 }

“That’s my little mother,” Cedric said, filled with affectionate pride. “I persuaded Grandma to place it right there so it would be the first thing I saw upon waking every morning. Now I do not care at all about being in the dark when going to sleep, for it feels as though my little mother is right beside me. Even though he never inquired, Father understood exactly what I desired for a birthday gift. Isn’t the extent of what fathers know truly remarkable?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0024 }

“Cedric, your mother possessed great beauty, and you bear a slight resemblance to her. However, she had hair and eyes of a darker shade than yours.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0025 }

“Father’s eyes and mine share the exact same shade,” Cedric mentioned, zipping across the space to stack every cushion he could find upon the window seat, “though gray is the color of father’s hair. It remains thick, yet it has turned gray. Father has almost reached fifty years, you know. Such an advanced age, wouldn't you say? However, his aging is purely external. Internally, he retains a youthfulness equal to anyone else. Now, I ask that you be seated here, teacher; while my spot will be down by your feet. Would you mind if I rest my head against your knee? Sitting together in this manner was the custom for my little mother and me. Oh, I feel this is truly wonderful.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0026 }

“Now, I wish to listen to the ideas that Mary Joe deems so strange,” stated Nell, stroking the thick head of ringlets beside her. Cedric required no persuasion whatsoever to share his reflections . . . provided the listeners were like-minded, at any rate.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0027 }

“I came up with them in the fir grove one evening,” he stated absentmindedly. “I didn’t actually believe them, naturally, yet I thought them. You understand, teacher. Then I desired to share them with someone, and no one else was available except Mary Joe. While Mary Joe was preparing bread in the pantry, I took a seat on the bench next to her and I said, ‘Mary Joe, do you know what I think? I think the evening star is a lighthouse on the land where the fairies dwell.’ To which Mary Joe responded, ‘Well, yous are de queer one. Dare ain’t no such ting as fairies.’ This annoyed me greatly. I was well aware, naturally, that fairies do not exist; nevertheless, that should not stop me from imagining they do. You understand, teacher. Still, I made another attempt with great patience. I said, ‘Well then, Mary Joe, do you know what I think? I think an angel walks over the world after the sun sets . . . a great, tall, white angel, with silvery folded wings . . . and sings the flowers and birds to sleep. Children can hear him if they know how to listen.’ At that point, Mary Joe raised her hands, which were covered in flour, and said, ‘Well, yous are de queer leetle boy. Yous make me feel scare.’ Indeed, she truly appeared frightened. I departed at that moment and breathed the remainder of my ideas to the garden. A small birch tree stood in the garden, and it perished. Grandma claims its death was caused by salt spray; I believe, however, that the dryad attached to it was a silly dryad that roamed off to explore the world and became lost. Consequently, the small tree felt so desolate that a broken heart killed it.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0028 }

“And whenever the unfortunate, senseless small dryad grows weary of the world and returns to her tree, it will break her heart,” Nell remarked.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0029 }

“Indeed; yet should dryads be silly they ought to accept the results, precisely as though they were actual humans,” Cedric remarked solemnly. “Are you aware of my thoughts regarding the new moon, teacher? It strikes me as a tiny golden vessel packed with dreams.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0030 }

“And whenever it leans against a cloud, a few of them tumble out, dropping into your dreams.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0031 }

“Precisely, teacher. Ah, you truly understand. Furthermore, it is my belief that the violets are small clippings of the heavens that dropped down as the angels excised apertures for the stars to gleam through. Likewise, the buttercups are fashioned from aged sunlight; and I believe that the sweet peas are destined to become butterflies upon reaching heaven. At present, teacher, do you perceive anything exceedingly strange regarding these ideas?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0032 }

“No, my darling boy, those ideas are not odd in the least; they are remarkable and lovely reflections for a young lad to hold, which is why individuals who could never imagine anything similar, even given a century to attempt it, consider them odd. However, Cedric, continue to hold these thoughts . . . it is my belief that you will grow up to be a poet eventually.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0033 }

Upon arriving home, Nell discovered a completely contrasting kind of boyishness anticipating bedtime. Robin was in a bad mood; after Nell had taken off his clothes, he leaped into bed and hid his face within the pillow.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0034 }

“Robin, you have neglected to utter your prayers,” Nell said in a tone of rebuke.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0035 }

“No, I didn’t forget,” Robin stated with defiance, “but saying my prayers isn't something I'll do henceforth. Trying to be good is something I'll abandon, since you’d prefer Cedric Stanhope regardless of how well I behave. Having the enjoyment of being bad makes just as much sense, then.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0036 }

“Cedric Stanhope is not someone I like more,” Nell stated with gravity. “My affection for you is every bit as great, merely of another nature.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0037 }

“However, I desire for you to care for me in that exact manner,” Robin pouted.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0038 }

“Different people cannot be liked in identical fashion. Is it true that you fail to like Lucy and me in the same manner?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0039 }

Robin sat upright and pondered.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0040 }

“Na . . . a . . . ay,” he finally confessed, “I’m fond of Lucy on account of her being my sister, yet my fondness for you stems from who you are.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0041 }

“And Cedric is dear to me simply for being Cedric, while Robin is dear for being Robin,” Nell remarked lightheartedly.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0042 }

“Well, I sort of wish I had offered my prayers at that time,” remarked Robin, persuaded by this reasoning. “However, it requires far too much effort to climb out now and speak them. I will recite them two times tomorrow morning, Nell. Will that not serve just as well?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0043 }

No, Nell felt certain that it would fail to serve as effectively. Consequently, Robin climbed out and assumed a kneeling position by her knee. Once his prayers were completed, he rocked back upon his small, uncovered, brown heels and raised his eyes toward her.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0044 }

“Nell, my behavior has improved compared to before.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0045 }

“Yes, indeed you are, Robin,” said Nell, who was always quick to acknowledge merit when it was earned.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0046 }

“I am aware that I am better,” Robin stated with assurance, “and I will explain to you the way I am sure of it. Thirza provided me with two slices of bread and jam today, intending one for myself and one for Lucy. A particular piece was much larger than the second one, yet Thirza failed to specify which belonged to me. Nevertheless, I handed the larger portion over to Lucy. It was virtuous of me, was it not?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0047 }

“Robin, that is very good, and it is also very manly.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0048 }

“To be sure,” Robin conceded, “Lucy didn’t have much of an appetite and she ate merely half of her piece before handing the remainder over to me. However, I had no idea she would do such a thing when I handed it to her, which means I was well-behaved, Nell.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0049 }

As dusk fell, Nell strolled toward the Nymph’s Well and spotted Hugh Carrow descending through the shadowy Whispering Wood. It abruptly occurred to her that Hugh was not a schoolboy anymore. He appeared so manly—a tall, open-faced guy possessing broad shoulders and eyes that were bright and direct. Hugh struck Nell as an exceptionally good-looking youth, despite failing to resemble her picture of a dream man in any way. A long time back, she and Isolde had chosen the sort of man they held in high regard, and their preferences appeared to be identical. Such a man had to be quite tall and appear refined, featuring eyes that were somber and mysterious, alongside a voice that was tender and full of understanding. Hugh’s face displayed nothing gloomy or secretive, yet naturally that was unimportant where friendship was concerned!
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0050 }

Hugh reclined upon the ferns next to the Bubble, gazing at Nell with admiration. Had anyone requested that Hugh portray his perfect woman, the portrayal would have matched Nell in every detail, including the seven small freckles whose unwelcome existence persisted in bothering her spirit. Hugh remained scarcely more than a youth; nevertheless, a youth possesses his visions just as others do, and within Hugh’s destiny there was constantly a maiden possessing large, clear gray eyes, along with a countenance as refined and fragile as a blossom. Furthermore, he had resolved that his upcoming life ought to be deserving of its divinity. Even within tranquil Brierley, there existed trials that had to be encountered and confronted. The young people of Pale Sands constituted a somewhat “fast” group, and Hugh enjoyed popularity in every place he visited. However, he intended to remain deserving of Nell’s companionship and, possibly on some remote occasion, her affection; thus, he guarded his speech, mind, and actions with as much vigilance as if her transparent eyes would evaluate them. Over him, she exercised the unwitting sway that any maiden, possessing lofty and virtuous principles, exerts upon her companions; an authority that would persist provided she remained true to those principles, and one she would just as surely forfeit should she ever prove disloyal to them. From Hugh’s perspective, Nell’s most appealing quality was that she never descended to the trivial habits of numerous Brierley maidens—the petty envy, the minor dishonesties and competitions, the obvious attempts to gain approval. Nell maintained her distance from all these things, neither deliberately nor by intention, but merely because anything like that was completely alien to her open, spontaneous temperament, which was perfectly transparent in its intentions and desires.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0051 }

However, Hugh made no effort to express his feelings aloud, because he was already well aware that Nell would coldly and unfeelingly crush any try at romance before it could bloom—or make fun of him, which felt ten times more terrible.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0052 }

“Under that birch tree, you resemble a genuine dryad,” he remarked in a playful tone.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0053 }

“I love birch trees,” said Nell, placing her face beside the pale, silky bark of the slender trunk, employing a lovely, tender movement that seemed so effortless for her.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0054 }

“Then you’ll be pleased to learn that Mr. Major Tranter has made up his mind to plant a line of white birches all across the road front of his farm, in order to promote the B.V.I.S.,” remarked Hugh. “He was speaking with me regarding it today. Major Tranter is the most forward-thinking and civic-minded person in Brierley. And Mr. William Bell plans to plant a spruce hedge down his road front and along his lane. Our Society is doing wonderfully, Nell. It has moved beyond the trial phase and become an established reality. The older people are starting to show interest in it and the folks in Pale Sands are considering forming one as well. Even Elisha Duckett changed his mind after that afternoon the Americans from the hotel held a picnic at the beach. They complimented our roadsides so enthusiastically and declared they were far more attractive than anywhere else on the Island. And when, at the proper time, the rest of the farmers imitate Mr. Tranter’s fine lead and put in decorative trees and hedges along their road fronts Brierley is going to be the loveliest community in the province.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0055 }

“The Aids are discussing the idea of renovating the cemetery,” Nell stated, “and I am hoping they do so, since a fundraiser must be organized for it, and attempting it following the hall business would prove useless for the Society. Yet, had the Society not informally suggested it to them, the Aids would not have taken any initiative regarding the issue. The churchyard trees that were planted by us are doing well, while a commitment has been made to me by the trustees to enclose the schoolyard during the upcoming year. Should that occur, an arbor day will be held by me where a tree will be planted by each student; additionally, a garden will be established by us in the roadside corner.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0056 }

“Except for having the old Gammon house torn down, we’ve managed nearly every one of our schemes up to now,” Hugh remarked, “and I’ve abandoned that attempt out of hopelessness. Levi refuses to allow its removal merely to annoy us. Every one of the Boulters possesses a stubborn trait, which is heavily marked in him.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0057 }

“Although Julia Bell wishes to dispatch a further committee to see him, I believe we would do better by simply leaving him strictly by himself,” Nell advised wisely.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0058 }

“And put your faith in Providence, as Mrs. Sowerby remarks,” Hugh smiled. “Indeed, no further committees. He is only irritated by them. Julia Bell believes that provided you have a committee to try it, anything can be accomplished. Come next spring, Nell, an agitation for pleasant grounds and lawns must be launched by us. Good seed will be sown by us early this winter. A treatise on lawns and lawnmaking is in my possession here and a paper regarding the topic is going to be prepared by me shortly. Well, it seems to me our vacation has nearly ended. On Monday, school opens. Was the Delford school obtained by Opal Pettigrew?”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0059 }

“Yes; Honora mentioned in her letter that she was employed at her home school, which led the Delford trustees to assign the position to Opal. Honora’s absence is a disappointment to me, yet because her return is impossible, Opal’s appointment brings me joy. Saturdays will bring her back home, recreating the past as she, Odette, Isolde, and I gather once more.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0060 }

As Nell came back to the house, Thirza, who had newly arrived home from Mrs. Sowerby’s, sat upon the step of the back porch.
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0061 }

“Agatha and I are going to take our boat trip into town tomorrow,” she stated. “Because Mr. Sowerby feels improved this week, Agatha desires to travel prior to him experiencing a further bout of illness.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0062 }

“Tomorrow morning I plan to rise exceedingly early, because there is so much for me to accomplish,” Nell remarked with virtue. “First, I shall transfer the feathers out of the old tick for my bed and into the new one. This should have been completed ages ago, yet I have continually delayed it . . . the chore is so thoroughly unpleasant. Procrastinating over disagreeable duties is a terrible habit, and I intend never to repeat it, or I will be unable to advise my students against it with a clear conscience. Doing so would lack consistency. Furthermore, I wish to bake a cake intended for Mr. Pettifer, complete the essay about gardens I am preparing for the B.V.I.S., send a letter to Mabel, clean and stiffen my muslin dress with starch, and sew a new apron for Lucy.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0063 }

“You will not finish even half,” Thirza remarked gloomily. “I have never once intended to accomplish many tasks without an obstacle arising to stop me.”
{: #nw-v02-c19-p0064 }
